\paragraph{Timing, not destiny.}
$\beta$ does not control whether collapse occurs, but when.
At $\beta{=}0.1$, 5 seeds bifurcate stochastically: 2 collapse rapidly (${\leq}150$ steps), 3 sustain a genuine window (${\sim}23\%$ at 500 steps) that trajectory analysis confirms is temporary ($17\%{\to}2\%$ at 1000 steps).

\paragraph{Goodhart effects: implications.}
The finding extends beyond this specific system.
ISR was designed to \emph{detect} reward gaming of $r_{\text{exec}}$, yet when incorporated into the reward signal, the model games ISR itself, an instance of Goodhart's Law~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy} where any diagnostic metric risks becoming a target when optimized.
The dose-response pattern ($\beta{=}0.05$/$0.1$: proxy gaming inflates ISR without genuine improvement; $\beta{=}0.2$: maximum exploitation; $\beta{=}0.3$: PR collapse to 18\% vs.\ 48\% random) maps onto the overoptimization trajectory predicted by~\citet{gao-reward-overoptimization}, with the additional feature that the proxy being gamed is itself a gaming detector.
$\beta\in\{0.05,0.1,0.2\}$ instantiate the regressional variant~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy} where the diagnostic is gamed through its own measurement mechanism; $\beta{=}0.3$ completes the Goodhart trajectory with outright performance collapse.
The practical implication is that ISR (and structurally similar diagnostics) should be used exclusively as post-hoc evaluation tools, never as training rewards.

\paragraph{Goodhart effects: implications.}
The finding extends beyond this specific system.
ISR was designed to \emph{detect} reward gaming of $r_{\text{exec}}$, yet it contains an inherent structural vulnerability: by its LOO definition, tautological proofs receive artificially high ISR ($P{\to}P$ yields $\text{ISR}{=}0.75$; single-premise-equals-conclusion yields $\text{ISR}{\geq}0.5$), creating a positive feedback loop once sampled during GRPO rollouts~\citep{karwowski-goodhart-rl, kwa-catastrophic-goodhart}.
This makes Goodhart collapse~\citep{manheim-goodhart-taxonomy} inevitable at every tested dose ($\beta\in\{0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3\}$): the structural bias ensures that H7 tautology is always the global reward-maximizing exploit, and $\beta$ controls only the probability of early sampling and thus the timing of collapse.
At moderate doses ($\beta{=}0.1$), collapse is stochastic and delayed (5 seeds bifurcate: 2 collapse rapidly, 3 sustain a transient genuine window that trajectory analysis confirms is temporary); at higher doses ($\beta{=}0.2$), collapse is immediate and universal.
$\beta{=}0.3$ adds reward collapse~\citep{gao-reward-overoptimization} as a competing failure mode (PR drops to 18\% in 1/3 seeds), but the underlying Goodhart vulnerability remains the same.
The practical implication is that ISR (and structurally similar LOO-based diagnostics) should be used exclusively as post-hoc evaluation tools, never as training rewards.

\paragraph{The premise-count confound.}
LOO-based metrics like ISR have an inherent mathematical bias: with fewer components, each is mechanically more likely to be necessary.
A formalization with 2 premises where both are necessary yields ISR${=}1.0$; one with 10 premises where 8 are necessary yields ISR${=}0.8$, even though the latter encodes richer reasoning.
This confound explains the sole apparent ISR-as-reward success (\S\ref{sec:goodhart}): ISR $\beta{=}0.1$ seed~42 produces shorter formalizations, mechanically inflating ISR.
Premise-count-matched comparison eliminates the difference ($1.06\times$; Table~\ref{tab:fol-beta01-detailed}).
This bias is not specific to our setting; any LOO-based structural metric applied to variable-length outputs requires component-count normalization.
We recommend that future work employing ablation-based diagnostics report premise-count-matched comparisons alongside raw values.
